tagline.text: The Philippines' largest coral reef, guarded by sharks and turtles

children.text: Apo Reef, in the middle of the sea west of Mindoro, is the Philippines' largest continuous coral reef and a nature park where fishing is entirely banned. Reef sharks, sea turtles, and large schools of fish make it a dream destination for divers, and it also offers deserted-island camping and snorkeling.
Apo Reef is a huge coral reef in the middle of the Mindoro Strait, about
30km

off the coast of Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro, on the west side of Mindoro Island. Coral reefs covering about 34 km² form two large ring shapes, enclosing a shallow lagoon at their center. It is the largest continuous coral reef in the Philippines, and is sometimes described as the largest continuous reef after Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

Three small islands sit on the reef. The largest, Apo Island, has mangrove forest, a sandy beach, a ranger station, and a lighthouse; to the east, Apo Menor (Binangaan) is a rocky islet, and Cayos del Bajo is a small islet built up from coral fragments. Since being designated a nature park in
, and managed as a strict no-take zone banning all fishing from
, the coral and fish populations, once damaged by overfishing and blast fishing, have visibly recovered. This value has also earned it a place on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List.

The underwater world is among the best in the Philippines. Whitetip and blacktip reef sharks, sea turtles, huge schools of jacks and barracuda, Napoleon wrasse, and rays appear often, and with luck you might spot a hammerhead or manta. Outside the reef, the wall drops away tens of meters, making for impressive drift dives.

Access isn't easy, though. As an uninhabited park with no hotels or restaurants, it requires advance booking through the Sablayan tourism office, boat charter, and camping preparations, and departures can be cancelled depending on the weather. It suits divers, snorkelers, and adventure-minded travelers looking for genuinely wild seas rather than easy comfort.

Management is shared by the protected area management office under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Sablayan local government, and only rangers on rotating shifts stay on the island. Figures vary by source, but the reef is described as home to more than 400 coral species and about 400–500 fish species, and 47 bird species have also been recorded. In 2022 it received the Blue Park Platinum Award from an international marine conservation organization. Apo Island covers about 22 hectares, and the lagoon on its north side is roughly
deep, making it well suited to snorkeling. The lighthouse on the island's northeast side stands on the site of a steel tower first lit around
; today a white solar-powered tower lights the shipping lane.
Riding the current along the outer reef wall, you can encounter reef sharks and large schools of fish. Current is strong in many spots, making this suitable for Advanced-level divers and above.
Even without a diving certification, you can snorkel the shallow water inside the reef and see healthy coral colonies and sea turtles. You must enter only in areas designated by the rangers.
Walk the boardwalk through the mangrove forest on the island's interior and observe the habitat of birds, crabs, and juvenile fish.
Around Apo Island's lighthouse you can see the striking contrast between the endless coral reef and the color of the sea. Check with the on-site rangers whether climbing it is allowed.
You can spend a night in tents or huts in a designated area near the ranger station. With no light pollution, the night sky is overwhelming.
A dedicated diving cruise departing from Batangas, Coron, or elsewhere lets you handle transport, lodging, and multiple dives all in one go.
Pandan Island, off the coast of Sablayan, is a small resort island good for snorkeling and rest before or after visiting Apo Reef.

Shark Ridge is a slope at 15–30m depth where you often see whitetip and blacktip reef sharks and rays, while Binangaan Drop-off is a sheer wall plunging into deep water where big groupers and tuna gather. Apo 29 is a seamount whose top sits at about 29m, suited to advanced divers hoping for barracuda schools and sharks. Hunter's Rock, away from the reef, is famous for sea snakes gathering during the June–July breeding season. There are around 20 dive sites in all, and where you go in is decided on the day by the current and the captain.

per person (based on 6 people; it costs more with fewer). You spend 5–6 hours round trip on the boat in a single day, so it is physically demanding.

, propeller aircraft have been banned from Manila's Ninoy Aquino Airport, so there are no direct Manila–San Jose flights. If departing from Manila, either take the P2P bus from NAIA Terminal 3, PITX, and elsewhere to Clark Airport (about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours

To go overland and by sea, take a bus from Manila to Batangas port (about
2–3 hours
, about
), then board a RoRo ferry to Abra de Ilog (about
2 hours 30 minutes
, about
). From Abra de Ilog port to Sablayan takes about
2–3 hours
by bus or van, and the bus costs about
. Getting from Manila to Sablayan takes a full day, so it is best to spend the first day on travel alone.

The Batangas–Abra de Ilog route is served by three operators, Island Water, Montenegro, and Orange Navigation, which together run about ten sailings a day, including many midnight and pre-dawn departures. Since boats to Apo Reef leave before dawn, choose a sailing that fits your arrival time, and check the latest schedule and fares, because fares can change with fuel prices.
The rule is to charter an authorized bangka through the Sablayan tourism office (ecotourism office). A boat for 10–15 people costs about
or more, depending on how long you stay and the size of the boat. It takes about
2–3 hours
from Sablayan port to Apo Island, and departures are usually before dawn. The tourism office requires booking at least 3 days ahead, and often only takes bookings during weekday office hours.
From the Sablayan pier to Pandan Island is about

per person by water taxi. The Pandan Island resort has a dive center and has run day trips and trips of one night or more to Apo Reef since 1991, so divers can leave their Apo Reef booking and transport to them. The resort's information also covers how to fly from Clark to San Jose Airport and continue from there, a direct bus from Manila's Parañaque terminal to Sablayan, and van transfer services from Manila and San Jose, so the most accurate way to get schedules and fares is to ask the resort directly.
If diving is the goal, a liveaboard departing from Batangas, Anilao, Coron, or elsewhere during the
March–June
season is the most efficient option. A 3–5 day itinerary is typical, and costs run into tens of thousands of pesos per person depending on the boat and itinerary.
If driving, load your vehicle onto a RoRo ferry at Batangas port, disembark at Abra de Ilog, and drive along the coastal road to Sablayan, about
2–3 hours
. Vehicle fares vary by vehicle type, so ask the shipping line. From San Jose Airport to the bus stop is about
by tricycle, and in Sablayan you get around the pier and town by tricycle. Boats to Apo Reef leave from a pier designated by the park office, so get the meeting point and time when you book.
Apo Reef sits in the middle of an open strait, so sea conditions determine whether the trip succeeds. The best time is from
March
to
May
, when winds are light and waves are low, giving a high chance of departure and often
or better underwater visibility. Most liveaboard diving seasons are scheduled around this period too.
From
November
to
May
is the dry season, and the sea is generally stable. However, on days when the northeast monsoon (amihan) is strong, waves in the strait can get high, and from
June
to
October

it is the southwest monsoon (habagat) and typhoon season, so sailings are often cancelled. Park authorities and the Coast Guard suspend visits entirely in bad weather, so in the off-season you should expect that even a confirmed booking can be cancelled on the day.
The island has little shade and strong sun. In the dry season, midday temperatures climb above 32°C, so pay close attention to hydration and sun protection.
The best time depends on your purpose. The Pandan Island dive center treats
December–June
as the diving season, while tourism guides name
February–mid-June
as the safest window. Sea snakes breed at Hunter's Rock in
June–July
, which is a treat for divers but can mean rough seas. In any season, the water temperature stays at 26–30℃ year-round, so you only need to pick the right wetsuit thickness.

There is no commercial lodging inside Apo Reef itself. Near the Apo Island ranger station there are a few park-managed huts (2–4 person), and camping is allowed in a designated zone. With few huts, they fill up quickly in peak season. Electricity is limited to solar lighting, making charging difficult, and showers depend on rainwater or limited fresh water.
Apo Island has only two huts for 2–4 people, equipped with bedding and a solar fan, at about

per hut per night. There is no electricity during the day; after sunset, from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., you can use solar power for lighting and charging. There is a toilet, but the water is mostly seawater, so bring your own drinking and washing water.
Before and after, stay at a guesthouse or small hotel in Sablayan town (about

per night). Pandan Island, offshore, has bungalow-style resorts, good for travelers wanting a quiet island stay. San Jose also has lodging near the airport, so you can choose based on your flight schedule.

There are no restaurants or shops on the island, so bring all food, water, and ice from the Sablayan market. Boatmen and helpers often cook rice and grill fish or meat, so confirm the cooking service and tip when you book. The Sablayan market has cheap fresh fish, mangoes, and bananas, and town restaurants serve Filipino home-style carinderia food for about
per person.
For comfortable lodging, the Pandan Island resort is the main choice. Rooms start at about
per night, and visitors who don't stay pay an entrance fee of about
and can use the resort from

. Large sea turtles can be seen up close in the water in front of the resort, which makes it popular with snorkelers. Sablayan has a mangrove forest park and a market, so it's a good place to combine shopping and a walk the day before departure.

Booking through the Sablayan tourism office is mandatory. Contact them at least 3 days ahead, during weekday office hours, to confirm your headcount, dates, and activities (snorkeling, diving, camping), and also check the latest conservation and diving usage fees, which change often.
Since chartering a bangka is costly, joining other travelers or a group arranged through the tourism office to share a boat can cut the per-person cost significantly.
ATMs are scarce in Sablayan and on the island, so it's best to bring plenty of cash from San Jose or Manila. All fees are paid in cash.
There's almost no phone signal on the island. It's a good idea to leave an emergency contact and your itinerary with family.
Dive gear rental is limited, so go through a dive center or bring your own gear. A personal mask and snorkel are worth packing.
Plan on at least 4 liters of water per person per day, and bring a cooler and ice as well.
Bring a dry bag, power bank, flashlight, insect repellent, and reef-safe sunscreen.
The Sablayan tourism office, the booking desk, takes inquiries only on weekdays,

. Contact them at (043) 458-0028, 0917 170 6723, or 0998 546 5917, and since contact details can change, also check the official Facebook page. Some reviews say an S-Pass registration about 72 hours before departure is also required, so ask whether any advance registration is needed.
The entrance and conservation fees are per-person rates, where one visit means within 48 hours, and a tour guide costs about
per group per day, charged separately. Divers pay an additional divemaster fee of about
. Park fees are revised every year, so confirm the latest amounts when you book.
Mask and snorkel rental is about

at the tourism office, so you can go without your own gear, but sizes are limited, so it's best to bring your own mask. The trip is 2–3 hours across open sea, so take seasickness medicine before departing.

Apo Reef is a fully protected zone. Collecting or touching coral, shells, or fish, and entering the water outside designated areas, are strictly banned and can carry fines and other penalties if caught.
Currents outside the reef can be very strong, so always dive with a local guide and avoid sites beyond your experience level.
Bad weather can ban departures, and your return from the island can also be delayed. It's best to leave at least a day of buffer before your return schedule.
The nearest hospital and decompression chamber are far away, so diving insurance is essential.
All trash must be taken back out, and fires may only be lit where rangers permit.
Chasing or feeding sharks is prohibited and dangerous.

The Coast Guard strictly checks the number of people aboard, so do not board a bangka that exceeds its capacity, and wear a life jacket during the voyage. Under the park's guidelines, you must not apply bug spray or regular sunscreen before entering the water. There is almost no fresh water on the island, so showers and dishwashing rely on seawater. Bring plenty of drinking water yourself, and tell the boatman in advance if you run short.
A small resort island about
15–20 minutes
from Sablayan port by bangka, good for snorkeling and rest.

A 925m natural boardwalk through Sablayan's 12-hectare mangrove forest, which won an award in a Department of Tourism competition in 2024. It makes a good alternative on days when rough seas cancel sailings.
A diving town in northern Mindoro. From Sablayan you have to go overland via Abra de Ilog or Calapan, so allow more than half a day. It's a good way to continue a Mindoro diving trip.
A northern Palawan island famous for wreck diving, often included together with Apo Reef in liveaboard itineraries.
A macro-diving destination in Batangas, also used as a departure point for Apo Reef liveaboards.
